About this simulation

On screen
Left: the mirror face-on, drawn to one fixed scale (the dashed circle is an 8 m mirror), with the light converging to the detector. Right: the 5″ × 5″ detector image, 21 × 21 pixels, with the 1″ seeing disc outlined; each pixel shows its count minus the measured mean sky level, with white at the star's expected peak at the end of the exposure. Recorded photons flash while the counts are small. Below the image, the true elapsed time. Inset: the exposure time needed against distance on log–log axes, with the present star as a dot.
Controls
Absolute magnitude ℳV of the star, its distance d (log scale, 10 pc to 1 Mpc), the mirror diameter D (log scale, 0.25 to 8 m) and the sky (dark site: sky in the seeing disc = magnitude 22; moonlit: 19). Changing any of them stops the exposure and clears the image. Expose records a fresh exposure; every playback lasts about 10 s on screen whatever its true length.
Measured
mV from the distance modulus; Ṅ★ and Ṅsky are recorded photons per second (η = 0.5, 1.0 × 1010 photons s−1 m−2 at magnitude 0); the exposure needed solves S/N = 10 with the mean sky subtracted and no dark current or read noise; S/N is the value reached at the clock's true time.
Assumptions
S/N = Ṅ★t / √((Ṅ★ + Ṅsky)t): all of the star's photons are counted together with the sky that falls in the 1″ seeing disc, and the mean sky level is known exactly. Photon counts follow Poisson statistics. There is no read noise, dark current or atmospheric extinction, so the shortest times are optimistic; a real detector needs at least a fraction of a second.

Guided Inquiry

1 · Moving the star away

Set ℳV to 4.8, close to the Sun's value of 4.83, the mirror diameter to 1 m, the sky to dark site, and the distance to 10 pc, so that mV = 4.8. Before moving the star, predict its apparent magnitude when it is moved to 100 pc.

2 · A bigger mirror

Keep the star at 100 pc with ℳV = 4.8 and the dark sky, with the mirror diameter at 1 m. Before changing the mirror, predict by what factor the photon rate Ṅ★ changes when the diameter is doubled to 2 m.

3 · Exposure for a bright star

Set the mirror back to 1 m and keep the star at 100 pc with the dark sky, and press Expose to see how long it takes to reach a signal-to-noise ratio of 10. Before moving the star, predict how the exposure time changes when the star is moved to 200 pc.

4 · Exposure for a faint star

Keep ℳV = 4.8, the 1 m mirror and the dark sky, and move the star to 200 kpc, where mV is about 26.3, far fainter than the dark sky's 22 in the seeing disc. Before moving it again, predict how the exposure time changes when the star is moved to 400 kpc.

5 · A moonlit sky

Keep the 1 m mirror and ℳV = 4.8. Before changing the sky, predict how switching from the dark site to the moonlit sky, which is three magnitudes brighter, changes the exposure time for the star at 100 pc and for the star at 200 kpc; then try both distances.

6 · A bigger mirror for a faint star

Set the sky back to dark site and keep the star at 200 kpc with ℳV = 4.8 and the 1 m mirror. Before changing the mirror, predict how the exposure time changes when the diameter is doubled to 2 m.

7 · What you found

From star to detector: mV = ℳV + 5 log10(d / 10 pc) sets the photon rate, Ṅ★ ∝ D2 × 10−0.4 mV.

For a star brighter than the sky in the seeing disc, t ∝ 1/Ṅ★, so t ∝ d2. For one fainter than the sky, t ∝ Ṅsky/Ṅ★2, so t ∝ d4, and a brighter sky costs time in proportion.

Either way a bigger mirror helps as 1/D2, which is why faint-object astronomy needs large telescopes at dark sites.

Counting Photons from a Distant Star

✦Learn this with the AI tutor

01

At a glance

A telescope turns starlight into a count of photons. This sim follows one star through a mirror to a small detector image, and asks what exposure gives a signal-to-noise ratio of 10.

What you'll learn

  • How a star's magnitude and distance set the apparent magnitude.
  • How the mirror and the sky set the photon rates.
  • How the count in an exposure sets the signal-to-noise ratio.
  • What limits the exposure for a bright star and for a faint one.
The sim's layout, drawn schematically: the mirror on a fixed scale, the detector image with its seeing disc, and the clock.

What's on screen

  • Mirror, drawn to one fixed scale: the dashed circle is an 8 m mirror. The light converges from it onto the detector.
  • Detector image: 21 × 21 pixels covering 5″ × 5″. Each pixel shows its count above the mean sky level. The dashed circle is the 1″ seeing disc, and orange flashes mark recorded photons.
  • Clock below the image: the true elapsed time, whatever speed the playback runs at.
  • Inset on the right: the exposure time needed against distance on logarithmic axes, with the present star as a dot.
See itWatch the opening exposure. Watch for: orange flashes landing inside the dashed seeing disc, one for each recorded photon.

Changing the star, the distance, the mirror or the sky stops the exposure and clears the image. Fixed: the detector records η = 0.5 of the photons, a magnitude-0 star delivers 1010 photons s-1 m-2 in the V band, and there is no dark current, read noise or atmospheric extinction, so the shortest times are optimistic: a real detector needs at least a fraction of a second.

03

The distance modulus turns absolute magnitude and distance into apparent magnitude

Magnitudes run backwards: a larger number is a fainter star. The absolute magnitude ℳV is the magnitude the star would have at 10 pc. Light thins as 1/d², and a factor of 100 in flux is 5 magnitudes, so the apparent magnitude at distance d is:

Notes equation (1.4): mV − ℳV is the distance modulus. The sim shows the result as Apparent magnitude mV.

Each factor of ten in distance adds 5 mag. The opening star, with ℳV = 4.8 (the Sun is 4.83), has mV = 4.80 at 10 pc and 9.80 at 100 pc. The apparent magnitude is the only thing the rest of the sim needs to know about the star.

Key idea. Distance enters through 5 log10(d/10 pc), so the star gets fainter by 5 mag for every factor of ten in d.
See itMove the opening star from 10 pc to 100 pc. Watch for: Apparent magnitude mV rising from 4.80 to 9.80 mag.
04

The photon rate grows with mirror area and falls as the star dims

A magnitude-0 star delivers about 1010 photons per second through each square metre in the V band (notes 1.19). A mirror of diameter D has area πD²/4, and a fraction η = 0.5 of the photons are recorded:

The rate falls by a factor 100.4 = 2.51 for each magnitude.

The same formula gives the sky's rate Ṅsky, with mV replaced by the sky's magnitude in the seeing disc: 22 at a dark site, 19 under the Moon. At the opening values the star delivers 4.721 × 107 photons/s and the sky 6.224. The sky's magnitude does not depend on d, so neither does Ṅsky.

Doubling D gives four times the collecting area.
Key idea. The mirror multiplies the star's rate and the sky's rate by the same area factor.
See itAt 100 pc, double the mirror from 1 m to 2 m. Watch for: both photon rates, from the star and from the sky, going up by the same factor.
05

Photons arrive at random, so the signal-to-noise ratio grows with the square root of the time

Photons from a steady source arrive independently at a constant mean rate, so the count in time t follows a Poisson distribution. Its mean is Ṅ★·t and its scatter is √(Ṅ★·t) (notes 1.21). The sky's photons in the seeing disc add scatter too; their mean level is measured and subtracted, but their scatter stays. With no dark current or read noise, the notes' (1.22) reads:

S/N is the star's mean count divided by the scatter of the whole count.

Setting S/N = 10 and solving for t gives the exposure the sim reports as Time needed:

The 100 is 10², the square of the target S/N.

The image is built photon by photon, so it is noisy until enough have arrived. The S/N so far readout is the value reached at the true elapsed time.

Key idea. S/N grows as √t, so an exposure four times as long doubles it.
See itExpose the star at 100 pc and watch the count build. Watch for: S/N so far climbing quickly and then more slowly to 10.0, as a bright spot emerges inside the seeing disc.
06

Time needed bends from d² to d⁴ once the star is fainter than the sky

The time needed has two limits. When the star beats the sky, the noise is the star's own, and since Ṅ★ falls as 1/d², t rises as d². When the sky beats the star, its scatter dominates, and since the sky's rate does not depend on d, t rises as d⁴ (notes problem 3):

The two rates are equal where mV = 22, at 27.5 kpc for the opening star at a dark site. That is the dashed "star = sky" line in the inset. The log–log slope is 2.00 at 100 pc and 3.96 at 200 kpc.

Time needed against distance for the opening star, 1 m mirror, dark site. Dashed lines: the two limits.
d D Sky

These controls move the sim too. The numbers come from the sim's own readouts.

Key idea. The exposure grows as d² while the star beats the sky, and as d⁴ once the sky sets the noise.
See itMove the star from 100 pc to 200 pc. Watch for: Time needed going up by a factor of 4.
See itNow move it from 200 kpc to 400 kpc. Watch for: Time needed going up by about 16, from 12.64 h to 199.5 h.
07

Moonlight and mirror size matter in different regimes

The Moon brightens the sky in the seeing disc from magnitude 22 to 19, a factor 101.2 = 15.8 in Ṅsky, and leaves the star alone. Where the star sets the noise, t hardly depends on Ṅsky: at 100 pc it rises by only 0.02%. Where the sky sets the noise, t is proportional to Ṅsky, so at 200 kpc it rises by 15.6, a little under 15.8 because the star still adds some noise.

Time needed under the Moon divided by time needed at a dark site, for the opening star and a 1 m mirror.

A larger mirror multiplies both rates by the same area factor, so t scales as D²/(D²)² = 1/D² in both regimes. For a faint star it is not 1/D⁴, because the mirror collects the sky as well. Doubling D divides t by 4.

Key idea. The Moon costs a faint star's exposure a factor of about 16 and a bright star's almost nothing, while the mirror helps both as 1/D².
See itPut the star at 200 kpc under the Moon. Watch for: Time needed reading 7.089 × 10⁵ s (196.9 h), 15.6 times the dark-site 12.64 h.
See itBack at the dark site, double the mirror at 200 kpc. Watch for: Time needed falling from 12.64 h to 3.161 h, a quarter.
08

Summary

In one line. A star's magnitude and distance set how many photons a telescope records; the sim turns that count into the exposure needed for a signal-to-noise ratio of 10.

Common mix-ups

  • "A larger magnitude is a brighter star." Larger mV is fainter, and each factor of ten in distance adds 5 mag.
  • "The exposure time always scales as d²." Only while the star beats the sky; beyond that t rises as d⁴, about 16 times longer from 200 kpc to 400 kpc.
  • "Moonlight wrecks every exposure." At 100 pc the time changes by 0.02%; at 200 kpc it rises by 15.6.
  • "A bigger mirror helps a faint star as D⁴." It collects the sky too, so t falls as 1/D²: 12.64 h falls to 3.161 h.

Things to try on your own

  • At a dark site, move d until the star's and the sky's photon rates match. They cross between 27 and 28 kpc, where mV = 22.
  • Set ℳV = 0. The "star = sky" line moves out to about 250 kpc, where the two rates are again about equal.
